item.title: Lumina simulation brings the early universe to life on a record-breaking scale
item.description: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Nancy Roman Space Telescope are revealing the universe's earliest chapters in detail. To help astronomers understand what they are seeing, researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian have developed "Lumina," one of the largest and most detailed simulations ever created of the early universe. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Experienced teachers are quitting or reducing their hours—they're struggling to cope
item.description: Teacher shortages are affecting school systems in countries across the world. Governments have responded with initiatives to attract graduates into teaching. While much attention has focused on increasing supply, far less attention has been paid to why experienced teachers decide to leave, despite the high costs of turnover in recruitment, training and lost continuity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Assessment tool helps schools look at students holistically
item.description: Researchers in the Neag School of Education are bringing a whole child screening assessment to a company that provides schools with a connected set of solutions that turn every student signal into timely, equitable, coordinated and measurable tools to track and manage supports. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Australian coral reefs face risk of collapse within 50 years without drastic action, global assessment finds
item.description: Every shallow-water coral reef ecosystem in Australia faces an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, driven largely by projected ocean warming, according to a global assessment. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Supercurrent enables the reading of quantum information without destroying it
item.description: One of the fundamental challenges of quantum computing is obtaining information from a quantum bit, or qubit. Unlike a conventional bit, which can be read repeatedly without altering its content, direct measurement of a quantum system typically causes the state to collapse before it can be determined. In other words, reading the information modifies it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Crows make decisions twice as fast as humans and monkeys
item.description: University of Tübingen researchers have shown that crows, when confronted with a visual choice, make a decision twice as fast as humans and monkeys. In the experiment, two carrion crows took just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction in which a dot pattern was moving and to indicate their choice—while maintaining a high degree of accuracy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Storms batter Europe, hitting power supplies, flights and phones
item.description: Storms battered northern Europe on Sunday cutting power to more than 150,000 homes, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights and silencing phone networks. Winds of up to 135km (84 miles) an hour were recorded in Argyll and Bute in western Scotland and fallen trees and power cables blocked roads and rail lines across the country. More than 82,000 homes in Britain, nearly 60,000 in France and at least 10,000 in Germany had power cuts inflicted by the passage of storms Boelo and Austen... Publicado también por: South China Morning Post. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Monarchs report their locations via… cellphone?
item.description: Who knew a monarch butterfly could borrow a cellphone to check in with friendly people he met on his journey? That is essentially what happens now that new technology has reduced the weight of a radio-pulse tag to less than half a gram (0.02 ounces). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Milky Way's disk grew 'upside down,' with younger stars forming in ever-thinner layers
item.description: The Milky Way is home to hundreds of billions of stars arranged in a glorious spiral pattern. But beyond the obvious spiral, our galaxy has other physical characteristics. It's divided into a galactic bulge, a galactic disk and a galactic halo. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How screening tools measure disadvantage may leave rural communities overlooked for public support
item.description: Whether a community is prioritized for public support can depend on how its needs are measured, according to new research from the University of New Hampshire. The study found significant differences in how government screening tools identify communities, particularly in rural areas where those differences could affect access to funding. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Patterns of polar vortices discovered in lead-free superlattices on silicon
item.description: A team at HZB has, for the first time, reported polar vortices in (BaTiO₃/SrTiO₃)₁₀ superlattices on silicon. These results expand the range of materials and substrates on which polar topological textures can occur and open up new options for incorporating complex ferroelectric states into silicon-based technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: El 6 de agosto, entre Aldeanueva de Ebro y Alfaro, varios viñedos cortaron los primeros racimos de tempranillo blanco. Era la vendimia más temprana de la historia de la Rioja . item.title: Protecting children from harm isn't enough—welfare systems must support healing through quality mental health care
item.description: In Quebec and across Canada, people working in child welfare do remarkable work to protect children and youth from maltreatment and to support families facing complex challenges. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A few seconds of loading time can push online learners off track
item.description: An online lesson takes an extra second to load. The wait may seem trivial, but in a study examining large learning platforms, these brief pauses were linked to unfinished assignments, lower scores and less time spent on the site. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Southern Africa's first known stenciled rock art found hiding in plain sight
item.description: Southern Africa has one of the most detailed and elaborate bodies of rock art anywhere in the world, from herds of running antelope to dancing men and humanoid beings with wings, hooves and horns. All are painted with fine brushstrokes or fingers. One thing this art lacks is stencils. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal the hidden danger of missing blood pressure medication
item.description: Missing blood pressure medication could mean losing much of its protection against heart attacks and strokes, according to an analysis of more than 91,000 people. Patients who consistently took their medication experienced an 11% reduction in major cardiovascular events, while those who missed too many doses saw little or no measurable benefit. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Just two drinks a day may be far riskier than you think
item.description: A major new study reveals that drinking just two alcoholic beverages a day is associated with a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of death from alcohol-related causes, challenging the idea that moderate drinking is harmless. Researchers also found no significant overall health benefits from alcohol, with risks rising as consumption increases. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Three giant black holes discovered in a galaxy from the dawn of time
item.description: Astronomers have discovered three actively feeding black holes inside a single galaxy more than 12.5 billion light-years away, revealing a remarkable scene from the universe’s infancy. Two of the black holes are separated by just 620 light-years and are expected to eventually merge, while a third lurks farther away. One weighs an astonishing 80 million suns, and another is growing faster than conventional theories predict. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Global underground CO₂ storage hit record 43.6 million metric tons in 2024 alone
item.description: The most comprehensive record yet of carbon dioxide stored underground through geological carbon dioxide storage has been published today, revealing that 43.6 million metric tons were sequestered in 2024 alone—a new annual record—and that 421.7 million metric tons have now been stored in the past three decades. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
item.description: Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
item.description: Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment. In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Sea cucumber–inspired gel could help heal damaged tissue in humans
item.description: Inspired by the ability of sea cucumbers to change the stiffness of their bodies, University of Waterloo researchers have developed a gel that could one day help repair damaged tendons and other soft tissues without leaving permanent material behind. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Low-dose aspirin linked to 70% lower dementia risk, but there's a catch
item.description: A common, inexpensive medication could hold an unexpected clue to preventing dementia. Researchers found that older adults with a specific genetic profile had a 70% lower relative risk of dementia when taking low-dose aspirin, even though previous studies found no overall protective effect. The discovery suggests that genetics could help explain why some people benefit while others do not. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Bust companies revived in ‘phoenix’ deals more likely to fail again, study finds
item.description: Exclusive: research for the Guardian shows ‘pre-pack’ deals with former management also pay far less to creditors The boss whose twice-bust business appears to be back Insolvent businesses reacquired by their previous management in “pre-pack” administrations are much more likely to fail again and tend to repay far less to creditors, research for the Guardian suggests. The study is the latest to raise questions about the practice of “ phoenixism ” – accounting’s controversial art of liquidating companies to allow directors to return with a new entity, free of debts. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.

Having learned his trade during the 1990s, he graduated to create his own firm at the turn of the millennium – which allowed him to bank millions of pounds in salary, dividends and loans and to buy assets including a grand house in Berkshire once owned by the comedians Dawn French and Lenny Henry. item.title: This mysterious mushroom makes people see hundreds of tiny humans
item.description: For nearly a century, people in distant parts of the world have reported a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, colorful humans moving through the real world. Now, scientists have identified a mushroom species, Lanmaoa asiatica, responsible for these extraordinary hallucinations in China and the Philippines. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Popular cannabis sleep gummies may have a hidden dark side
item.description: A cannabis-derived ingredient commonly found in sleep gummies may be more habit-forming than previously thought, with new research showing that repeated exposure caused tolerance and withdrawal symptoms in mice. Scientists warn that CBN may carry risks similar to THC, although its long-term effects in humans remain largely unknown. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Astronomers may have discovered the first moon beyond our Solar System
item.description: Astronomers have uncovered evidence of a bizarre, potentially historic discovery: the first moon ever detected beyond our Solar System. Unlike familiar moons, this mysterious object is at least as massive as Jupiter and orbits a brown dwarf, which itself circles a star. The unusual arrangement challenges traditional definitions of planets and moons, leaving scientists unsure what to call it. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden flaw that challenges 40 years of superconductor science
item.description: A superconducting material studied for 40 years has turned out to be far more complex than scientists believed. Advanced 3D imaging revealed a hidden patchwork of crystal structures, with unusually wide boundaries that may weaken superconductivity. The discovery challenges decades of scientific assumptions and could explain why some superconductors outperform others. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Mediterranean diet may boost tiny proteins that protect the heart and brain
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising new clue to why the Mediterranean diet is so good for the heart, brain, and healthy aging. Researchers at USC found that older adults who closely followed the diet had higher levels of two tiny proteins, humanin and SHMOOSE, produced by the mitochondria, the energy-producing structures inside cells. These proteins have been linked to protection against heart disease, Alzheimer's disease, and age-related damage. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: De acuerdo con el diario francés ‘Le Monde’, el hombre que mató a una persona e hirió a cinco el viernes 23 de octubre le dijo a la policía que escogió a sus víctimas por el color de su piel y que su misión era vengar a los comerciantes saqueados durante los violentos disturbios que sacudieron a Francia la semana anterior. En una revisión en su residencia en Yvelines, los investigadores habrían encontrado un ejemplar de ‘Mein Kampf’, el libro escrito por Adolf Hitler. Mientras tanto, las localidades afectadas, Trappes y La Verrière, intentan procesar el terror vivido el día anterior. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Solar storm delayed a train by 16 minutes in 1848, not 1841: How scientists solved a 155-year-old mystery
item.description: A fascinating correction has emerged from the archives concerning a train delay in Exeter. Initially reported incorrectly, researchers have clarified that the incident actually transpired on October 18, 1848. This revelation was achieved through the analysis of railway records and contemporary newspapers, alongside geomagnetic data, which pointed to a significant solar storm influencing the delay during that time. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Bell pepper colors reveal differences in sweetness, nutrients and ripeness
item.description: Raw, grilled, roasted, stuffed—there are many ways to enjoy bell peppers, also called capsicums, sweet peppers or paprika. Bell peppers originated in Central and South America and belong to the nightshade family along with tomatoes and eggplants. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tests reveal why titanium additions do not fully prevent pitting corrosion in stainless steel
item.description: Stainless steel is widely used for its corrosion resistance, but it is not invincible. In environments containing chloride ions, such as seawater, pitting corrosion can occur. These pits often start at tiny particles called inclusions embedded in the steel. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The Tasmanian garden helping people with dementia live well
item.description: A gardening program in Hobart is helping people with dementia reconnect with the world around them. Researchers hope the lessons from these outdoor spaces will help more people continue to live well. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: Single X-ray pulse reveals plasma nanostructures across scales with one camera
item.description: Understanding instabilities and turbulence in plasmas is one of the key challenges across a wide range of plasma research fields, including nuclear fusion, astrophysics and laser-plasma physics. In plasmas, slight disturbances can grow due to instabilities, and energy is transferred between structures of various sizes due to turbulence. These phenomena give rise to structures ranging from very small to large, which significantly influence the overall motion and energy flow of the plasma. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mientras discutimos qué especie introducir, el oso pardo sigue expandiéndose por el noroeste de la península Ibérica
item.description: Desde los años 80 y hasta final del siglo XX, el oso pardo cantábrico le vio las orejas al lobo: estuvo a punto de desaparecer, llegando a alcanzar un mínimo histórico que hizo saltar las alarmas ante su extinción. Y sin embargo, hoy vuelve a ocupar un territorio amplio en la península Ibérica, como documenta el CSIC. El retorno del oso pardo . Un estudio de la Estación Biológica de Doñana ha reconstruido cómo ha cambiado su área de distribución desde 1982 hasta alcanzar los 17.000 kilómetros cuadrados y por qué. item.title: How flare ribbons reveal hidden solar explosions on the sun
item.description: Many topics in astronomy and astrophysics are esoteric. There's not much of a relationship between something like the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way and the life of a regular person going about their business. But the sun is different. Its presence in our lives is inescapable. Its behavior, especially its flaring, has an impact. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 'One-positron cyclotron' could test a key prediction of the Standard Model
item.description: The positron is the antimatter counterpart of the electron, identical in mass but carrying an equal and opposite electric charge. Like the electron, it also behaves like a tiny bar magnet, and according to a key prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics, its magnetic moment should be exactly equal and opposite to the electron's. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newly identified protein pathway helps HIV stay hidden despite treatment
item.description: Current HIV medicines are effective at suppressing the virus in the blood. However, HIV can remain "asleep" or dormant inside certain immune cells and in the brain. These hidden pockets of virus, called HIV reservoirs, are the main reason HIV cannot be cured with today's treatments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nanoscale alloy redesign tackles cold brittleness for potential deep-space and deep-sea applications
item.description: Metallic materials used in extremely cold environments must maintain high strength, ductility and fracture toughness to support applications in aerospace, clean energy, superconducting systems and deep-space exploration. However, traditional alloys often suffer performance degradation at ultralow temperatures because of the long-standing trade-off between strength, ductility and toughness. Although metals may become stronger at lower temperatures, they can also become more brittle and prone to fracture. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Seabird family tree predicts which species accumulate plastic better than diet, global analysis finds
item.description: What seabirds eat might seem like a good starting point for identifying species that tend to accumulate plastic in their digestive systems. Yet a recent global analysis suggests that mapping the evolutionary relatives of birds could offer better clues than their diets or feeding methods alone. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Could lowering high blood pressure be as simple as stimulating your ear?
item.description: A small device that gently stimulates nerves through the ear could offer a new way to tackle stubborn high blood pressure. In a clinical trial of 63 patients already taking medication, the treatment proved safe, easy to use at home, and well tolerated. Although it did not significantly outperform a placebo overall, patients with more severe hypertension showed promising reductions in blood pressure. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A hidden bias in human language challenges 70 years of science
item.description: A groundbreaking study challenges 70 years of assumptions about how human language works. By analyzing billions of word uses, scientists discovered that meaning is organized around power, danger, and order rather than emotion alone. Even more surprisingly, human language shows a powerful hidden preference for safety, suggesting that our words may reflect ancient survival instincts. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
item.description: Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are rewriting scientists' understanding of how our Solar System formed. New evidence suggests that Bennu was born where material from the inner and outer Solar System mixed, with Jupiter playing a surprising role in shaping its formation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists propose a way to detect dangerous “mirror life” before it exists
item.description: Scientists have proposed a way to detect “mirror life,” a hypothetical form of life that could pose serious risks to humans, animals, and ecosystems if artificially created. Using special fluorescent molecules and a type of polarized light also used in 3D movie technology, researchers believe they could distinguish ordinary organisms from their mirror-image counterparts. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
item.description: The Sun’s seemingly peaceful regions are hiding a surprisingly complex magnetic world. Using a balloon-borne telescope high above Earth, scientists discovered delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the solar atmosphere, apparently shaped by twisting motions on the Sun’s surface. They also mapped magnetic fields inside towering jets of solar material, revealing how those fields change with height. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: These tiny snakes roll four times faster than they slither
item.description: Tiny snakes in Southeast Asia have mastered an extraordinary escape technique: rolling across the ground at speeds up to four times faster than ordinary slithering. Scientists discovered that dwarf reedsnakes accomplish this feat through precisely coordinated body movements that allow their bodies to rotate while their heads remain remarkably stable. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Cleaner brick kilns cut pollution, but gains did not reach workers, research finds
item.description: Relatively simple changes to the way traditional brick kilns operate in Bangladesh can reduce pollution, save fuel and improve the quality of bricks they produce. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New long‑clawed British dinosaur is the first of its kind in Europe
item.description: The fossilized skull of a new species of mysterious meat-eating dinosaur from the Isle of Wight has been rediscovered in the collections of the Natural History Museum after over 100 years in storage. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Your blood could reveal inflammatory bowel disease 10 years before diagnosis
item.description: A major study has uncovered hidden warning signs of inflammatory bowel disease in the blood up to 10 years before diagnosis. Researchers discovered distinct antibody patterns that could help predict who would later develop Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, even distinguishing people at risk of more complicated disease. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden switch that burns fat and blocks new fat cells
item.description: Scientists have discovered that switching off a protein called Mitch makes human cells burn more fat and prevents new fat cells from developing. The breakthrough builds on experiments in mice that showed remarkable resistance to obesity and improved muscular endurance, raising hopes for a new approach to weight-loss treatment. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Swinging virtual lightsabers and punching improve pattern-based learning in VR tests
item.description: Punching a virtual response box or swinging a virtual lightsaber can dramatically improve learning on certain tasks, according to new research from Florida Atlantic University's College of Engineering and Computer Science, which challenges long-standing assumptions about how people learn. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China study suggests animal sacrifice may have been part of ancient Sanxingdui rituals
item.description: Animal sacrifice has played a major role in human history, from mythological stories about Odysseus to modern rituals such as Nepal’s Gadhimai Festival. The tradition also dates back to ancient peoples we know little about. A research paper published in the Journal of Archaeological Science in late August suggests that the enigmatic Sanxingdui people likely practised animal sacrifice. To reach this conclusion, researchers identified what appeared to be a sacrificial pit based on the spatial... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Typhoon Champi knocks out power to thousands in Taiwan
item.description: Emergency crews scrambled on Saturday to restore power to tens of thousands of homes in Taiwan after Typhoon Champi's fierce winds battered the island, with the storm moving toward China and Japan. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Eating late at night linked to up to 30% higher risk of liver disease, study finds
item.description: Recent research emphasizes the concerning link between late-night eating and liver diseases. A comprehensive study involving nearly 200,000 participants over a median span of 16 years found that those who dined late displayed increased cases of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and cirrhosis. The underlying mechanisms linking meal timing to liver health are still not well understood, warranting further exploration into how eating habits impact liver well-being. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.description: NASA is moving fast on its plans to build a moon base and return astronauts to the lunar surface in as little as two years. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China carries out in-depth investigation of Turkey’s largest rare earth deposit
item.description: Chinese researchers have mapped the complex geological evolution of Turkey’s Kizilcaoren deposit, offering fresh insights into the country’s most significant known rare earth reserve while dampening expectations over its commercial potential. Although the findings shed light on how rare earth elements accumulate in carbonatite-related formations, the researchers concluded that the site was unlikely to emerge as a major global alternative to existing producers any time soon. Lead scientist... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Surveying the genetic battlefield to uncover the rules of rapid evolution
item.description: The Malik Lab thrives on competition. But for HHMI investigator Harmit Malik and his team at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, it's the genomes—not the people—that are in conflict. The lab studies rapid evolution—the genetic changes that happen in a species over a few generations rather than thousands of years. These fast changes are often fueled by genetic conflicts—competitions between different entities trying to maximize their success at the expense of another. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: This 150-million-year-old bird had dinosaur teeth and a strange secret
item.description: A 150-million-year-old fossil discovered in China reveals a bizarre early bird with sharp teeth, a dinosaur-like claw, and a body built for life on the ground rather than flight. Scientists believe it represents the earliest known example of flight loss in birds, overturning assumptions about how these animals evolved. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Child-led citizen science helps Ecuadorian community tackle beach pollution and shape environmental decisions
item.description: Pollution from human-generated waste in marine ecosystems has reached critical levels, with cigarette butts (CBs) among the most persistent and harmful pollutants. Globally, an estimated 4.5 trillion cigarette butts are discarded annually, making them the most common type of litter on beaches over the past three decades. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Habitat explains Finnish animal distributions better than climate, study finds
item.description: Researchers at the University of Helsinki wanted to understand which is the dominant factor for species occurrence and abundance: the climate or habitat-related variables, such as their natural state and the share of land shaped by human activity. Solutions to mitigate biodiversity loss depend on the answer to this question. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Glioblastoma breakthrough reveals how brain cancer cells become more aggressive
item.description: Scientists discovered that the thick, sticky fluid surrounding glioblastoma tumors can make brain cancer cells smaller, more flexible, and better at invading surrounding tissue. Even more troubling, some of these changes persist after the cells leave the thick fluid, revealing a previously overlooked mechanism that could help this deadly cancer spread. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Power cuts and sleep: Students link load shedding to anxiety, disrupted rest and lower grades
item.description: South Africa endured its worst year of load shedding (scheduled power cuts by the country's utility, Eskom) in 2023. The power went off on 335 of the year's 365 days, often several times a day. Since then, the country has gone more than a year and a half without these planned power cuts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Glowing plants reveal immune responses around infection sites via two colors
item.description: Researchers at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (LMS) have developed a new way to make glowing biological reporters more accurate, allowing scientists to track gene activity in living plants over days, weeks and potentially even months and years. The approach could help researchers study how plants respond to disease, pests and environmental stress, while opening the door to similar applications in animal and human disease models. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Darwin is the only Australian capital where house prices are still rising, but some property researchers says the market could soon turn. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
